newsitem.title: JAPAN: Oil stats show Japan losing interest in Oman crude.
newsitem.headline: Oil stats show Japan losing interest in Oman crude.

text.p: Japanese oil companies -- with their sophisticated refining equipment -- are rapidly losing their appetites for medium Omani crude, a fact underscored by Japanese government data released on Friday.

Monthly import statistics released by the Ministry of International Trade and Industry (MITI) showed about 925,500 kilolitres (kl) of crude oil were imported from Oman in March, a 21.6 percent drop from February and 33.6 percent from March 1996.
With demand down, Omani crude is now trading at a steep discount of as much as 20 cents to the official selling price.
"I don't think it's a particularly good grade for refineries here," said a Western trader who deals heavily in Omani crude.
Traders said that Oman, which has a low sulphur content of 0.8 percent, was attractive to many refineries in Asia which do not have the secondary refining facilities to remove the unwanted sulphur.
But Japanese refiners have the secondary facilities so they can buy crude which is cheaper but has a higher sulphur content.
"Every month we check around...there's usually not much buying interest from Japanese refiners," the Western trader said.
"Take this month, there's not one refiner that's really looking to buy Oman in Japan," he added.
Gulf crudes for June-loading, which is the current active trading month, have been weak almost across-the-board.
Oman has been hit particularly hard, with Japanese traders only showing a cursory interest.
Moreover, China and South Korea, traditional buyers of the crude, have turned to buying West African cargoes, whose prices are tied to Brent.

Traders said Oman is one of the crude oil grades that Japanese oil companies have started to buy less of on a term basis, part of a move to economise that began with the introduction of oil market deregulation in April 1996.
Japan's imports of Omani crude amounted to 14.7 million kl in 1996, down 12.2 percent from 1995, MITI statistics showed.
Japan imports some 85 percent to 90 percent of its crude oil on a long-term basis.
One leading Japanese oil company said it used to purchase as much as 40,000-50,000 barrels-per-day (bpd) through term contracts, but had cut back that volume dramatically.
"We virtually take no (Omani crude on a term basis) now," a trader with the company said.
Most Asian crude oil buyers, including China, Thailand and South Korea, have term contracts with Oman. These countries have replaced Japan as the principle purchasers of the crude.
Oman's loss has been Iran's gain.

Imports of Iranian crude in March, for example, jumped 37.1 percent year-on-year to 3.32 million kl. Iranian Heavy, the largest volume of Iranian crude grade imported by Japan, has a sulphur content of 1.6 percent.
Imports of crude oil from the Middle East accounted for 81.1 percent of all Japan's imports in March.
The United Arab Emirates topped the list of exporters having shipped about 6.0 million kl of crude oil to Japan in March.
